hints: Count how many acidic protons citric acid has by looking at the three $\text{COOH}$ groups plus the $\text{OH}$ group.
Recall what happens to an $\text{O-H}$ bond when Na reacts, what replaces H in $\text{COONa}$ and $\text{ONa}$, and what gas causes fizzing.
Work out how many Na atoms are needed for four $\text{O-H}$ groups and how many $\text{H}_{2}$ molecules this produces.
walkthrough:
Spot the two types of O-H that react**
Look at citric acid closely. You have three carboxylic acid groups, $\text{COOH}$, and one alcohol group, $\text{OH}$. Both contain an $\text{O-H}$ bond that is acidic enough to react with sodium metal. The $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-OH}$ of the alcohol carbon skeleton stay in place, only the H of each $\text{O-H}$ is replaced.

Write the sodium salts**
Think of sodium taking the place of that H. Each $\text{COOH}$ becomes $\text{COONa}$ and the $\text{C-OH}$ becomes $\text{C-ONa}$. So the product skeleton is identical to citric acid except all four $\text{OH}$ hydrogens are now $\text{ONa}$ groups: $\text{C(CH}_{2}\text{COONa)}_{2}\text{(COONa)(ONa)}$.

Balance Na and hydrogen gas**
Each $\text{O-H + Na}$ gives $\text{O-Na}$ plus half $\text{H}_{2}$. With four $\text{O-H}$ groups you need 4 Na atoms: $$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}_{7} + 4\text{Na} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{O}_{7}\text{Na}_{4} + 2\text{H}_{2}$$ That $\text{H}_{2}$ is the fizzing you see in the table.

Final answer: Citric acid + 4Na → $\text{C(CH}_{2}\text{COONa)}_{2}\text{(COONa)(ONa)}$ + 2$\text{H}_{2}$
All three $\text{COOH}$ groups converted to $\text{COONa}$ and the alcohol $\text{OH}$ converted to $\text{ONa}$ in skeletal structure.

hints: Use the formula $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{3}$ with one $\text{COOH}$ and one $\text{OH}$ to work out how the three carbons must be arranged.
Think where the $\text{OH}$ must sit on a 3 carbon chain so that carbon has four different groups attached.
walkthrough:
Build a molecule that fits all the clues**
X has the same functional groups as citric acid, so it must contain $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{OH}$. With only $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{3}$, there is room for just one of each: $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{4}(\text{OH})(\text{COOH})$ essentially. It also fizzes with Na, confirming $\text{O-H}$ is present, and it is oxidised by dichromate, so the alcohol cannot be tertiary.

Place the OH to create chirality**
Try $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)COOH}$. The middle carbon is joined to $\text{CH}_{3}$, H, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COOH}$, four completely different groups. That is a chiral centre, so mark it: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C}^{*}\text{H(OH)COOH}$. In skeletal form this is a 3 carbon zigzag with $\text{OH}$ on the middle carbon and $\text{C=O}$ with $\text{OH}$ on the end carbon.

Final answer: Skeletal formula: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)COOH}$ (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) drawn in skeletal form.
Chiral carbon (C-2, bearing $\text{CH}_{3}$, H, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COOH}$) labelled with *.

hints: Look back at the citric acid structure and classify its alcohol group as primary, secondary or tertiary by counting carbons attached to the C-OH carbon.
Recall which classes of alcohol can be oxidised by $\text{H}^{+}/\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$ to cause the orange to green change.
walkthrough:
Classify the alcohol in citric acid**
Find the $\text{C-OH}$ in citric acid. That carbon is attached to three other carbons (two $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups and one $\text{COOH}$ group). That makes it a tertiary alcohol. Tertiary alcohols have no H on the $\text{C-OH}$ carbon, so they cannot lose hydrogens to form $\text{C=O}$ without breaking C-C bonds.

Classify the alcohol in X**
In $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)COOH}$, the $\text{C-OH}$ carbon is attached to two carbons only ($\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{COOH}$), plus one H. That is a secondary alcohol. Secondary alcohols are oxidised by warm acidified dichromate to a ketone: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)COOH} + [O] \rightarrow \text{CH}_{3}\text{COCOOH} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$ The dichromate is reduced, giving the orange to green colour change.

Final answer: Citric acid contains a tertiary alcohol group which is not oxidised, so dichromate remains orange.
X contains a secondary alcohol group which is oxidised to a ketone, reducing orange $\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}^{2-}$ to green $\text{Cr}^{3+}$.

hints: Recall the feature in X that allows it to exist as non superimposable mirror images.
Recall the other common feature involving a double bond that prevents free rotation and requires different groups on each carbon.
walkthrough:
First feature, the chiral centre**
Picture your left and right hands as mirror images that cannot be laid exactly on top of each other. Molecules do the same when they have a carbon with four different groups. That gives a pair of optical isomers, which is exactly why X exists as a pair of stereoisomers.

Second feature, the rigid double bond**
A $\text{C=C}$ cannot rotate like a single bond. If each carbon of the $\text{C=C}$ carries two different groups, swapping their positions in space gives different arrangements, cis-trans or E-Z isomers. That is the second key feature, even though X itself uses the first one.

Final answer: 1. A chiral centre / carbon attached to four different groups / non superimposable mirror image (optical isomerism).
2. A $\text{C=C}$ double bond with two different groups attached to each C atom (cis-trans / E-Z isomerism).

hints: Compare what must stay the same (atoms present) with what must change (how they are joined) for isomers that are not stereoisomers.
walkthrough:
Separate formula from structure**
Think of having the same set of building blocks but joining them in a different order. A structural isomer has exactly the same numbers of each atom, so the molecular formula $\text{C}_{3}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}_{3}$ is identical, but the bonds connect differently, giving a different structural formula. For example, an ester or a different hydroxy acid with no $\text{O-H}$ to react with Na would fit part (d).
Final answer: Molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae / different arrangement of atoms.
